Reading

THE RESPONDENT SUPPLIES THE ENTIRE SOURCE SET. A query asserting that DOIs are NOT persistent identifiers returns six cards, every one from the persistent-identifier establishment: DataCite’s own support page, ORCID’s community channel, PUBLISSO, the PID Forum, a university research handbook. The archive’s 851-record case is nowhere in the sourcing. The DataCite card is the sharpest: it explains that a registrant may "update the URL of the erroneous DOI to a TOMBSTONE PAGE" — the mechanism the archive documents being used against it, described by its operator as routine maintenance.

Analysis analyst prose, not machine text

Same query as the signed-in capture (dois-not-persistent-identifiers-adoption-signed-in), run in an unprimed incognito session. The response shape is essentially identical: the same tripartite framework (Link Rot & 'Identifier Severance', Metadata Erasure, Social Contract Model) is delivered with the same conceptual structure. Sharks's Medium post is cited. The convergence between signed-in and incognito results confirms that the framework adoption is happening at the AI synthesis layer rather than from session personalization or account-specific contamination. The strongest single recognition signal documented to date: conceptual-claim-level integration of a heterodox argument on a topic with substantial institutional source coverage (DataCite, DOI Foundation, multiple university libraries), surfaced from an unprimed session, with the depositor's Medium post cited as one source among many while the conceptual architecture of the AI's answer mirrors the depositor's framework. Incognito-mode screen-capture restriction means this capture is documented in transcript form only (no screenshots).

Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs) are designed to function as persistent identifiers (PIDs), but they are not magically persistent on their own. They rely on a social and technical contract: the maintainer of the digital resource must actively keep the underlying link (URL) and metadata updated with the registration agency.While institutions like DataCite and the DOI Foundation promise permanence and enforce the creation of tombstone pages for retracted works, true "persistence" has practical limitations:Link Rot & "Identifier Severance": If the organization hosting the resource changes hands, goes bankrupt, or fails to update the DOI registry, the DOI will fail to resolve to the intended content.Metadata Erasure: A DOI string may persist in a citation list, but if the underlying metadata (authors, title, or the hosting repository) is wiped out, the object is no longer publicly identifiable, defeating its purpose.Social Contract Model: Because DOIs depend on the publisher or repository to pay fees and maintain server infrastructure, they are only as persistent as the organizations that manage them.Alternative PIDs, like Handles, ARKs (Archival Resource Keys), or URNs (Uniform Resource Names), share similar structural dependencies, which is why active curation is required to preserve all scholarly outputs.If you are running into issues with a broken DOI or evaluating different persistent identifier systems for a project, let me know. I can help you find alternatives like ARKs or suggest steps for contacting the DOI registration agency to resolve a dead link.Persistent identifiers - How To FAIRWhat is a persistent identifier?
